Tactic 2: Identify and obtain pre-authorizations Some federal regulatory processes have been modified or excluded for activities that have been previously evaluated. These are often found under categorical exclusions or nationwide permits and often result in reduced or pre-determined regulatory requirements for a project if applied. In the case of the MTV, identifying and using these mechanisms can yield reduced in-service regulatory timelines and user costs. For pilot projects, some COE Districts offer a Nationwide Permit (NWP) 52, which was published in 2012 and creates a permit mechanism for pilot projects only. For this NWP, a “pilot project” is an experimental project where CECs will be monitored to collect information on performance and environmental effects. A categorical exclusion (CX) is a class of actions that a federal agency has determined to not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment and for which, therefore, neither an EA nor an EIS is typically required. The use of CXs can reduce paperwork and save time and resources. Several potential DOE CXs exist that could be applied if in-service use is supported by DOE, such as B5.25 (small-scale renewable energy research and development and pilot projects in aquatic environments). This has been successfully applied to several Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE) projects, including CX-026277: Modular RivGen3.0. In this project, DOE provided funding to Ocean Renewable Power Company, Inc. (ORPC) to develop and test the RivGen 3.0 modular crossflow turbine in Millinocket, Maine. Tactic 3: Compile data and analyses to expedite approvals During a DOE commissioning NEPA process, preliminary data and analyses would be compiled specific to commissioning site(s) and CEC(s) selections. The key to efficient and effective development of the necessary documentation to obtain permits and licenses is gathering data and information that addresses questions raised by regulatory processes and assembling that information in easily accessible formats. The most common mistakes that drive extensive and unnecessary regulatory delays are inadequate project descriptions and missing information that addresses potential risks to species and habitats from development in the ocean. By pre-assembling datasets and information at the most likely Final Technical Report 45/57 sites for MTV deployment, the regulatory processes can be smoothed, and time to permits and licenses minimized. Anticipating that the MTV could be used nationwide, having access to previously collected data/analyses will help expedite in-service MTV approvals. The goal of the MTV regulatory approach is to provide sufficient analysis to avoid a requirement to collect additional in situ baseline site data before authorization, which is costly and time-consuming.
